sources.text: Show HN: Asking – A simpler customer support inbox for small teams Hi HN — I’m William, a frontend engineer from Brazil, and for the past few months I’ve been building Asking. Asking brings customer conversations from different channels into one place. It is intended for small teams that need a proper support workflow but don’t want the cost and complexity that usually come with larger platforms. To be transparent, Asking is built on top of Chatwoot. I’m not trying to present its messaging infrastructure as something I created from scratch. I’m using it as a foundation and building a more opinionated product around it, with simpler onboarding, inbox configuration, subscriptions, email setup, and a less overwhelming experience overall. The project started with a question: how much customer support software does a small business actually need? Many products are initially simple, but become expensive as the team grows. Others provide every feature imaginable, but require small companies to adopt workflows and concepts they may never need. With Asking, I’m trying to find a better balance: enough structure to manage customer support properly, without turning it into an enterprise system

Deno is joining Cloudflare

The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers.

Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on celld to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog.)

The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year:

Release: ttok 1.0

I released ttok 0.4, ran uv tool upgrade ttok, piped a file into the new version... and realized that it was defaulting to the GPT-4 tokenizer when it should very clearly default to GPT-5/GPT-6 instead!

I figured switching the default was a reasonable excuse to finally ship a 1.0.

OpenAI haven't actually confirmed that GPT-6 uses the same tokenizer as the GPT-5 family yet - there's an angry issue about it - but I found this commit by William Liu which reports on an experiment he ran confirming that the tokenizers are likely the same:

All seven GPT models (5.5, 5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, 6 Astra/Sol/Luna) report 44,794 tokens and match each other on every one of the 31 fixtures. GPT-6 introduces no input-count change on this corpus.

sources.text: At a high level, coding agents have a basic architecture: an LLM calls tools in a loop, while carrying forward the required context. But as the open laptop meme illustrates, modern agent harnesses have frustrating limitations if they’re not able to be managed in the cloud . sources.text: Show HN: GenClass, A 10 MB in-browser model that catches bugs that never throw Daybot is ranked number two in Canada, after Shopify, for making e-commerce stores. With a lot of AI-generated stores like Daybot's, we ran into the issue of the CSS sometimes not being up to standard. For example, the text and the background might end up the same color. I've also seen that race conditions often happen on the client side and are never caught in test cases, because they aren't tested under load, or because clients sometimes do actions that are just random. With AI-generated code becoming more popular, we thought that an AI agent that runs in the browser at runtime, is very lightweight, catches bugs like race conditions, stops unintended behavior, and gets better the more users use it would completely change the game. Now you can even run code faster. So I want you to try it out. You can add it with one line. It's published as an npm package. Please let me know what you think. Product URL: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@genclass/runtime

sources.text: Show HN: Evaluate and improve your agent steering Hi HN, excited to be open sourcing two tools that we have built over past few months which helps to understand your own work with AI coding agents Agent Desk is a local macOS app which allows you to browse your sessions across all top coding agents - Claude code, cursor, codex, github copilot, Kiro, Antigravity. You can find sessions by your projects, revisit those conversations, understand and inspect your entire harness - rules, skills, hooks, subagents. https://github.com/tetriz-ai/agent-desk Session Intelligence is a go library which helps structure and analyse your session transcripts using your own LLM. It can help understand missing context, repeated corrections, if session reached its goal and where is effort being wasted. sources.title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
sources.text: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects. Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units. GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked). Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models. GitHub: https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks. Product URL: https://parsimony.lasu.dev/

sources.title: Show HN: Factory DS, A Factorio-Like Game for the Nintendo DS
sources.text: Show HN: Factory DS, A Factorio-Like Game for the Nintendo DS Hi HN, I'm Ronan. I love the Nintendo DS but ran out of games that kept me hooked, so I tried porting the kind of game I play today: a factory game in the spirit of Factorio, on a 67 MHz ARM9 with 4 MB of RAM. I had never written code for the DS, and I built it with Claude Code. I wrote the specs, the design and the balancing, and Claude wrote most of the C. The post goes through how that worked, and through the technical parts I found the most fun: - a 2048x2048 world that is never stored: terrain is computed from (x, y), only the player's changes are kept in a hash table - night done by changing the 256-color palette instead of redrawing the screen - power grids and pipes computed per network with union-find (there is a small step-by-step animation in the post) - trains with schedules, block signals and pathfinding, plus redstone-like logic gates - a headless Mac build of the game with a text interface, so AI agents could play ~470 test sessions and even help balance the game You can download the ROM (English and French) and play it on a flashcart or in melonDS. Product URL: https://ronangaillard.github.io/posts/factor

sources.text: Show HN: Commit-Aware Router, route LLM traffic around your AI/cloud commitments LLM routers can optimize for different factors like price, latency, quality, etc. Enterprises tend to have prepaid AI credits, minimum-spend agreements, cloud commitments, or commercial ceilings across OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS, Azure, and other providers. We’ll call these “AI commits”. This project is designed to consider the state of an enterprises’ current AI commits and use it to inform LLM routing decisions alongside other common variables (price, performance, etc.). This is an early PoC built using LiteLLM. Target audience would CFOs, Strategic Finance, FinOps, Cloud Finance, and AI Platform folks who care about making sure AI commit minimums are met, and maximums are not exceeded. Would love any feedback from folks! Product URL: https://github.com/tejaspruthi/CommitAwareRouter
